tip: Chaining 주다 (juda = give) after a verb turns it into a favor for someone: 보여 주세요 (boyeo juseyo) = show it – for me. Korean marks who benefits right inside the verb.
들고 타다 (deulgo tada) is literally 'hold and board' – Korean chains two verbs where English says 'carry on'. 들고 탈 거예요 (deulgo tal geoyeyo) = I'll board holding it.
동안 (dongan = for/during) comes AFTER the time span, not before: 한 학기 동안 (han hakgi dongan) = for one semester, literally 'one semester during'.
Clock hours take native Korean numbers: 아홉 시 (ahop si) = nine o'clock. Minutes switch to Sino-Korean numbers, so a single time of day mixes both counting systems.
Some verbs have a full honorific replacement, not just a polite ending: for a teacher, 말하다 (malhada = to speak) becomes a different verb – 말씀하세요 (malsseumhaseyo).
'Different FROM' uses the with-particle in Korean: 한국하고 달라요 (hangukago dallayo) = different from Korea, literally 'different with Korea'.
A verb + -는 방법 (-neun bangbeop) = 'the way of doing it': 인사하는 방법 (insahaneun bangbeop) = the way of greeting. The describing verb comes before 방법, not after.
입에 맞다 (ibe matda) is literally 'fits the mouth' – food that suits your taste 'fits'. 입에 잘 맞아요 (ibe jal majayo) = it suits me well.
말이 통하다 (mari tonghada) is literally 'words get through' – communication as an open channel. 안 통해서 (an tonghaeseo) = because they don't get through.
Korean expresses missing a person as wanting to see them: 보고 싶어요 (bogo sipeoyo) = I want to see (them) = I miss them. The everyday 'I miss you' is literally a wish to see.
챙기다 (chaenggida = look after) chained before another verb adds 'make sure to': 챙겨 봐요 (chaenggyeo bwayo) = I make a point of watching, not just watch.
께 (kke) is the respectful version of 에게 (ege = to): 부모님께 (bumonimkke) = to my parents. The particle itself carries the politeness.
-이라서 (-iraseo) after a noun means 'because it is': 첫 해외여행이라서 (cheot haeoeyeohaeng-iraseo) = because it's my first trip abroad – no separate word for 'is' needed.
The 는 (neun) tucked into 생각하지는 않아요 (saenggakajineun anayo) makes the denial partial: with 꼭 (kkok = necessarily), it reads 'I don't necessarily think so', not a flat no.
-지는 않지만 (-jineun anchiman) = 'not exactly X, but': 확실하지는 않지만 (hwaksilhajineun anchiman) = I'm not certain, but... The 는 makes the denial partial.
Koreans rarely say a flat no – 아닌 것 같아요 (anin geot gatayo) = 'it seems not so' turns disagreement into an impression, which is the polite default.
-는 건 아니에요 (-neun geon anieyo) = 'it's not that I...': 반대하는 건 아니에요 (bandaehaneun geon anieyo) denies only the framing, not the whole idea.
왜냐하면 (waenyahamyeon) opens 'because' but can't end the sentence – it must close with -기 때문이에요: 부족하기 때문이에요 (bujokagi ttaemunieyo). Reason marked at both ends.
Influence is something you give in Korean: 영향을 줘요 (yeonghyangeul jwoyo) = literally 'gives influence'. Same with stress or help – 주다 (juda = give) does the work.
-지 마세요 (-ji maseyo) is the polite 'please don't': 믿지 마세요 (mitji maseyo) = please don't trust. It attaches to the bare verb stem, whatever the verb.
꼭 (kkok = necessarily) plus a negative = 'not necessarily': 꼭 그렇다고 볼 수는 없어요 (kkok geureotago bol suneun eopseoyo) = you can't necessarily see it that way.
귀를 기울이다 (gwireul giurida) is literally 'tilt an ear' – leaning in to listen. 귀를 기울여야 해요 (gwireul giuryeoya haeyo) = we should lend an ear.
-려고 (-ryeogo) marks purpose – 'in order to': 이해하려고 (ihaeharyeogo) = in order to understand. The goal comes before the trying, the reverse of English order.
-하였음을 (-hayeosseumeul) packs a whole clause into one formal noun: 결심하였음을 (gyeolsimhayeosseumeul) = 'that I have decided' – the compressed style of official notices.
-십시오 (-sipsio) is the most formal 'please do', used in announcements and official documents: 제출해 주십시오 (jechulhae jusipsio) = please submit. Everyday politeness uses -세요 instead.
삼가 주시기 바랍니다 (samga jusigi baramnida) = 'we ask that you refrain' – the fixed formula on Korean signs. 삼가다 (samgada) prohibits without ever saying 'don't'.
말씀을 올리다 (malsseumeul ollida) is literally 'offer words upward' – the humble replacement for 말하다 (malhada = to say) when addressing honored guests.
새옹지마 (saeongjima) is 'the frontier old man's horse': it ran off (bad), came back with another (good), his son fell off it (bad). Fortune keeps flipping – the whole saying in four syllables.
천고마비 (cheongomabi) is literally 'sky high, horses fat' – autumn air is clear and the harvest fattens the horses. Four syllables that mean the perfect crisp season.
The frame 것은 ... 때문이다 (geoseun ... ttaemunida) means 'the reason X is Y': 지켰던 것은 (jikyeotdeon geoseun) opens the puzzle, 때문이다 closes it with the cause.
The -(으)ㅁ (-eum) ending turns a whole clause into a formal noun: 일어설 수 있음 (ireoseol su isseum) = 'being able to stand back up'. Written style packs ideas into nouns.
Korean puts the whole describing clause BEFORE its noun: 겨우 탄 비행기 (gyeou tan bihaenggi) = the 'barely-boarded' plane. English trails with 'that I barely boarded'; Korean front-loads it.
-(으)며 (-myeo) is the written cousin of spoken -(으)면서 (-myeonseo = while): 가로지르며 (garojireumyeo) = while crossing. Novels pick -며; conversation picks -면서.
-고 나서 (-go naseo) alone means 'after' – the extra 야 (ya) sharpens it to 'only after': 옮기고 나서야 (omgigo naseoya) = only after I transferred.
-기란 (-giran) sets up 'as for doing X' and expects an easy/hard verdict: 두려워하지 않기란 (duryeowohaji ankiran) = as for not fearing... (no easy thing).
The -았/었음 (-eosseum) ending turns a past clause into a noun of fact: 사람이었음 (saramieosseum) = the fact that they were people. Written Korean states realizations this compactly.
것인지도 모른다 (geosinjido moreunda) = 'it may well be that...' – 지도 모르다 (jido moreuda), literally 'don't even know if', is Korean's soft hedge for musings.
-(으)ㄴ데도 (-ndedo) = 'even though it's so': 법인데도 (beobindedo) = even though that's how it tends to be. One ending does the work of a whole 'and yet' clause.
-던 것이다 marks a literary reveal: 아내였던 것이다 (anaeyeotdeon geosida) = 'she was, it turns out, his wife'. The 것이다 (geosida) ending stamps the sentence as the story's key fact.
시작하다 (sijakada = to begin) needs the -기 (-gi) noun form before it – you begin 'the stacking', not 'to stack': 쌓기 시작했다 (ssaki sijakaetda) = began stacking.
-(으)ㄴ 것이 lets a whole past clause be the sentence's subject: 꺼내지 못한 것이 (kkeonaeji mothan geosi) = 'his failing to take it out' – that entire event does the changing.
-던 바 (ba) is formal written shorthand for 'given the fact that': 높았던 바 (nopatdeon ba) = given that they were high. Bureaucratic prose favors this ending.
